rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi pairs al-Takāthur with al-Qāriʿah because both address what matters in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Sūrah al-Tak āthur forms a pair with S ūrah al-Q āri‘ah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qāriʿah teaches that good deeds alone weigh in the Hereafter: more good deeds bring salvation, while greater evil brings lasting doom despite worldly treasure.
rows.anchor: will have weight in the Balance of Justice.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This sūrah warns people who spend life competing for wealth and luxuries that they will face the dreadful consequences of forgetting accountability.
rows.anchor: outdo one another in the acquisition of wealth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People will answer for what they acquired, how they acquired and spent it, and whether they used their abilities and blessings to please God or gratify their desires.
rows.anchor: They would be inquired about everything they had acquired, the manner in which it was acquired

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb alhā means to allure or deceive people.
rows.anchor: means “to allure” and “to deceive.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takāthur means striving to outdo one another in wealth and children.
rows.anchor: means “to strive to outdo one another in wealth and children.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because families secured tribal defense, the family with most members received that responsibility, spurring rivalry in both wealth and family size.
rows.anchor: a family was responsible for the defence and security of a tribe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pre-Islamic Arabs took pride in surpassing others in wealth and having large families.
rows.anchor: they used to take a lot of pride in not only outdoing one another in wealth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Modern family planning has shifted the social preference toward smaller families, yet an unlimited standard of living keeps the desire for wealth insatiable.
rows.anchor: widely acclaimed concept of family-planning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because greed grows faster than living standards, the race for material gain has no end and distracts people from the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: unmindful to the other important realities of life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zurtum derives from a noun meaning simply to see, not the Urdu sense of a sacred visitation; here it means seeing the graves, or being consigned to them.
rows.anchor: simply means “to see,” contrary to its connotation in Urdu

rows.speaker: Ḥam āsī poet
rows.claim: A Ḥamāsī poem describes seeing one’s land after long absence and finding one’s friends gone while the land remains unchanged, illustrating the sense of visiting or seeing.
rows.anchor: To quote a Ḥam āsī poet:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Arabs kept and boasted of records of their dead, that custom is not what this verse means.
rows.anchor: the Arabs used to keep an account of the graves of their people and proudly mentioned them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grave image preserves the rhyme and conveys pity for people who forfeited the Hereafter’s reward through endless rivalry for wealth.
rows.anchor: adopting this particular style is firstly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated warning confronts people who mistake material success for life’s only goal and tells them this life is not the end.
rows.anchor: all that one must strive for

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unseen Hereafter is the life people should truly strive for, and they will soon witness it themselves.
rows.anchor: this life whose charms have allured them so much is not the end

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled stress makes the warning stronger and signals that rejecting a prophet sent directly to a people brings punishment in both worlds.
rows.anchor: The double stress in these verses is to make this warning more effective

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repetition warns a people who reject their directly sent prophet to reform or face humiliation in this life and the next as their fate is decided.
rows.anchor: a nation which rejects and denies the message of a prophet directly assigned towards them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vagueness of “you will come to know” itself carries an unmistakable threat.
rows.anchor: is too evident to be described in words.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People’s carefree pursuit of wealth stems from disbelief in Judgment; then they will see Hell and answer for blessings squandered against God’s wishes.
rows.anchor: It is attributed to their lack of belief in the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If they truly believed in Judgment, they would have prepared for it instead of pursuing material gain.
rows.anchor: If they had a true belief in the Day of Judgement, they would never have indulged

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators agree that the conditional apodosis is omitted, but do not make the following verses subordinate to the opening condition.
rows.anchor: almost all the commentators agree to this, but they do not consider the subsequent verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi instead reads all the later verses as subordinate to the opening law clause and supplies the omitted result: knowing these realities would have changed their attitude.
rows.anchor: you would never have adopted this attitude.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement about seeing Hell functions as the object of “if you knew with certainty,” rather than as a new sentence; the emphatic lām reinforces certainty.
rows.anchor: It is not a new sentence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic particle attached to the verb confirms the certainty of seeing Hell.
rows.anchor: is meant to emphasize this certainty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowledge of Judgment is already established by Qur’anic signs, human intuition, and nature, so evading this evidence gives no excuse and merits punishment.
rows.anchor: in the manifest verses of the Qur’ ān, in our own intuition, as well as in every phenomenon of nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Certain knowledge from evidence is possible in this world, but certainty by directly seeing hidden realities, ʿayn al-yaqīn, belongs only to the Hereafter; claims otherwise are baseless.
rows.anchor: can be obtained in this world as well

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final verse remains subordinate to the conditional clause: knowing that people would be questioned for every blessing means knowing they would be punished for misuse and ingratitude.
rows.anchor: punished for misusing these blessings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-naʿīm covers all human skills, organs, abilities, means, and resources; people owe gratitude and must use these gifts within God’s limits rather than become devoted to them.
rows.anchor: all the skills and capabilities, as well as all means and resources God has blessed us with

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because wealth is a special sense of al-naʿīm in this sūrah, people answer for lawful acquisition and proper spending; hoarding and worshipping wealth leads to the fate described in al-Humazah.
rows.anchor: wealth, which is one of the connotations of the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an often omits a conditional result when context makes it clear, using brevity to carry a fuller meaning.
rows.anchor: There are many places in the Qur’ ān where this style is adopted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted result is a final warning to reconsider one’s policies and life in light of undeniable realities, and to redirect effort from material pursuits toward the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: the omitted part which is left to the imagina tion of the reader, is actually a final warning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omission exemplifies how Qur’anic brevity can carry profound meaning in very few words.
rows.anchor: how effectively the Qur’ ān uses brevity to conceal profound meanings in a minimum number of words

none: The page contains only a closing formula, prayer of gratitude, and date.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿAṣr follows al-Takāthur’s warning against wasting life amassing wealth; people would have used life wisely if they knew they must answer for this great blessing.
rows.anchor: waste all their lives in planning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This sūrah explains life’s real value and the factors that make it a path to salvation or a cause of eternal punishment.
rows.anchor: the real value and importance of life is divulged

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath points to a lifespan as a person’s real investment: using it well earns God’s favor, while wasting it brings Hell; time can serve either the person or Satan.
rows.anchor: this time period is like a sword which can be used in both ways

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only the present is available to shape; the past cannot return and the future is hidden, with its own demands.
rows.anchor: which is hidden to him and no one knows its extent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person cannot defer a present obligation to an uncertain future.
rows.anchor: defer his present obligation to the future.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah briefly lays out the way to use life well and thereby fulfill the individual and collective duties on which salvation depends.
rows.anchor: his eternal salvation depends

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s guidance to organize personal and collective life for success in the Hereafter is condensed into these three verses.
rows.anchor: the message which is conveyed by one hundred and fourteen sūrahs of the Qur’ ān has been succinctly put forth in three verses

rows.speaker: Im ām Sh āfi‘ ī
rows.claim: Imām Shāfiʿī is reported to say that reflective reading of Sūrah al-ʿAṣr alone would suffice for people.
rows.anchor: Im ām Sh āfi‘ ī has pointed by saying that if people only read S ūrah al-‘A ṣr while reflecting on its contents, it will suffice for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening particle wa means that time bears witness, and ʿaṣr means a period of time.
rows.anchor: means “a period of time.”

rows.speaker: Ḥam īd al-Dīn Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī distinguishes ʿaṣr from dahr: ʿaṣr emphasizes time moving swiftly forward and is commonly used for time that has passed.
rows.anchor: my mentor Ḥam īd al-Dīn Far āhī has written while presenting his research

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays’s verse uses ʿaṣr for a past age, asking whether those who lived then now enjoy good fortune.
rows.anchor: good fortune for those who were in the time of the past.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras describes an ʿaṣr when he saw himself riding a young, beautiful she-camel.
rows.anchor: Fa dh āka ‘a ṣru ṇ wa qad ar ānī

rows.speaker: Im ām Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī says ʿaṣr evokes both past events and their swift passage, prompting belief in divine recompense and diligence in using time.
rows.anchor: Im ām Far āhī summarizes the discussion thus:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath recalls historical examples of divine reward and punishment and urges people to use fleeting moments to gain an eternal kingdom rather than a curse.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has directed our attention to the various events of history

rows.speaker: Im ām Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī says earlier peoples received exact recompense: virtue brought ascendancy, while oppression and disorder led to destruction after a clarifying respite; the oath warns later people of the same law.
rows.anchor: Im ām Far āhī has explained this point in the following words in his exegesis:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Time is a person’s real investment and its speed its defining feature; trusting it while ignoring worldly transience and judgment is naïve.
rows.anchor: the real investment a person has is that of time

rows.speaker: Im ām Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī compares people who fail to use time to a merchant who admires melting ice instead of selling it for profit, and later regrets the loss.
rows.anchor: Im ām Far āhī cites an example to explain this reality:

rows.speaker: Im ām Far āhī
rows.claim: The speed of time also offers hope: a wise person can endure brief self-discipline to gain eternal pleasure, while one lured by worldly pleasure forfeits it.
rows.anchor: In this regard, Im ām Far āhī has directed our attention to another aspect:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lifespan is valuable yet rapidly consumed, so everyone is losing except those who believe and do good deeds.
rows.anchor: all people are in a state of loss except those who

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith and righteous action fulfill life’s purpose: defying Satan brings mutual pleasure with God and Paradise, while surrendering to Satan’s lures forfeits an extraordinary favor.
rows.anchor: the Almighty will be pleased with him

rows.speaker: Im ām Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī traces īmān to amn, with senses of giving peace, attesting or trusting, and having absolute faith; muʾmin is also a divine name because God grants safety to those who seek refuge.

rows.speaker: Im ām Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī defines religious īmān as certainty joined with humility, trust, and adherence: a believer accepts God’s signs and commands, submits to Him, and accepts His decisions.
rows.anchor: Im ām Far āhī, whilst explaining the meaning of īmān in his exegesis, has written

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Righteous deeds follow as faith’s necessary corollary: true faith should shape actions, and their absence shows that faith has not taken firm root.
rows.anchor: When true faith is engendered in a person, just as its radiance lights up his inner-self

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi explains that inward faith can be self-deception, so words alone do not prove belief; a person’s deeds must also testify to faith.
rows.anchor: For this reason, two testimonies were needed to be required for it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic address to those who believe with the tongue calls them to believe through their deeds.
rows.anchor: O you who believe with the tongue! Believe through your deeds.

rows.speaker: Im ām Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī explains ṣāliḥāt as actions that enable apparent and inward, worldly and religious, individual and collective development toward human potential.
rows.anchor: Im ām Far āhī writes: God has regarded good deeds to be ṣāli ḥāt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Righteous deeds accord with God’s wise design for the universe’s collective order, since the world is governed by purposeful prudence rather than play.
rows.anchor: deeds will be regarded as righteous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since human beings naturally live in families and society and receive material and moral support there, they must care for others’ welfare rather than remain indifferent.
rows.anchor: by his very nature, he has a gregarious temperament; he is always a part of a family and member of a society

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers must urge one another toward truth and patience: ḥaqq includes faith as God’s greatest right and righteous acts concerning God and other people.
rows.anchor: īmān is included to the utmost in al-ḥaqq because it is the right of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience is needed both to remain steadfast in truth and to call other people toward it; believers therefore counsel one another to persevere in these duties.
rows.anchor: without adhering to perseverance and patience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary defines ḥaqq as what exists and endures, then gives three common senses: certainty, what reason acknowledges as true, and moral obligation.
rows.anchor: The word ḥaqq is used primarily for what exists and continues to exist.

rows.speaker: Im ām Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī derives the special sense of helping the poor from ḥaqq’s general sense: aid is a right incumbent on the capable, and iḥsān is recognized as maʿrūf.
rows.anchor: After citing various arguments from the Qur’ ān in favour of these three meanings, Im ām Far āhī writes:

rows.speaker: Im ām Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī says Arab patience means resolve and tenacity, not helpless weakness, and cites Ḥātim Ṭāʾī’s poetry as evidence.
rows.anchor: Whilst presenting his research on the word ṣabr , Im ām Far āhī writes:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥātim Ṭāʾī’s cited poem uses language of endurance through severe trials, illustrating patience as fortitude.
rows.anchor: wa ghamratu mawti ṇ laysa f īhā haw ādatu ṇ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic example of patience in adversity, illness, and war identifies these as the chief sources of hardship.
rows.anchor: three situations to display ṣabr

rows.speaker: Im ām Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī says ḥaqq opens the way to virtue, while ṣabr blocks evil; ḥaqq is the desired good and ṣabr the drive to attain it.
rows.anchor: A summary of all these details is that ḥaqq opens the door to all virtues and ṣabr closes the door to all evils

rows.speaker: Im ām Far āhī
rows.claim: Farāhī says ḥaqq and ṣabr comprehensively combine virtues and good deeds, with steadfastness sustaining a virtue after it is attained.
rows.anchor: the real thing is steadfastness once a virtue is attained

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith is presented as the foundation and nucleus, with righteous deeds following as its explanation.
rows.anchor: many branches sprout from a root

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Love of ḥaqq produces patience: honor and resolve rise with the value of what is loved, so people defend it and God’s cherished right provokes His anger when damaged.
rows.anchor: The reason for the Almighty’s anger and fury is also because He holds ḥaqq dear
